sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Spatio-temporal data receives increasing attention, due to
the widespread application of new-generation information
technology, which has become an important foundation for
the construction of new digital infrastructure and has strategic
value in promoting the new development of the industry.
Currently, some spatio-temporal prediction models have been
proposed and widely applied in various fields and tasks.
Existing research on spatio-temporal sequence predic-
tion primarily focuses on traffic prediction. Early stud-
ies mainly emphasize time series data while neglecting

spatial correlation, leading to inaccurate prediction results,
especially in cities or regions with complex road network
structures. Therefore, researchers have explored how to
effectively model the spatial characteristics of traffic flow by
integrating both temporal and spatial features to improve the
accuracy of traffic flow prediction. V oort et al. [1] Enhanced
the accuracy and efficiency of traffic flow forecasting by
using Kohonen maps, a self-organizing mapping neural
network, in conjunction with the ARIMA time series model.
Ma et al. [2] adopt a two-dimensional spatio-temporal matrix
to transform the dynamic traffic data into images that depict
the spatio-temporal relationships of traffic flow. They apply
CNN to these image data. However, CNN is primarily
suitable for processing structured data, and the topological

structure of roads and the unstructured nature of traffic flow
may result in the loss of some valuable information when
using CNN to extract spatial features of traffic flow. With the
rise of graph neural networks, researchers have introduced a
series of models based on graph neural networks to address
extracting features from unstructured information. Graph
convolutional neural networks have been applied in traffic
prediction and have achieved significant results.
By combining graph neural networks (GNNs) with recur-
rent neural networks (RNNs) to construct spatio-temporal
sequence prediction models, we can effectively capture
spatial and temporal features of geographical topological
graphs. This approach addresses modeling geographical
location networks, learning flow data propagation patterns,
and adapting to dynamic changes. Lee et al. [3] propose a
richer multi-graph convolutional framework, which is able
to capture complex dynamic properties in road networks,
such as non-Euclidean space and directional features,
enabling it to perform well in urban roads. Bai et al. [4] by
combining GCN with GRU, the modeling of time series
and road network topology is achieved. And the weights
are dynamically adjusted according to the importance of
different historical time points, so as to capture the global
traffic change trend more accurately. Wu et al. [5] design
the Multi-Temporal Graph Neural Network (MTGNN)
framework tailored for modeling multi-dimensional time
series data. Feng et al. [6] propose a novel deep learn-
ing approach based on multi-component spatio-temporal
graph convolutional network for traffic flow prediction.
Zhao et al. [7] introduces a comprehensive prediction method
combining graph convolutional networks (GCN) and Gated
Recurrent Units (GRU). They use GCN to learn complex
topological structures to capture spatial dependencies while
employing GRU to capture dynamic changes in traffic data,
effectively capturing temporal dependencies. On the other
hand, Gu et al. [8] propose an entropy-based grey relational
analysis method to extract spatial dependencies in traffic
flow. They also utilize a two-layer recurrent neural network
to predict lane-level speeds rapidly. Du et al. [9] introduce
Astrologer, a graph neural Hawkes process that integrates
spatial information and influences between different events to
capture event propagation from historical events on graphs.
The fundamental idea of Astrologer is to combine the
conditional intensity function of the Hawkes process with
graph convolutional recursive neural networks. Subsequently,
Du et al. [10] introduce a model named Nostradamus, which
captures the propagation of interesting events from historical
events with spatio-temporal features using a hyperbolic graph
neural Hawkes process. The core concept of Nostradamus
combines the conditional intensity function of the Hawkes
process with hyperbolic graph convolutional recursive neural
networks. The above methods allow for a comprehensive
consideration of spatial and temporal features, thereby
enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of traffic flow
prediction.
Similar to traffic flow prediction, electricity load fore-
casting also needs to consider spatio-temporal sequence
characteristics. As is known, power load forecasting is related
to many factors, involving climate, population mobility,
special events, and historical loads. Above spatio-temporal
sequence prediction models are not applicable to power load
forecasting as it requires the use of multi-dimensional time
series data, while the existing spatio-temporal forecasting
methods can only handle one-dimensional time series data
and one-dimensional spatial series data. In addition, previous
frameworks often rely on given spatial adjacency graph
and complex mechanism to capture spatial and temporal
correlations. However, limited representations may hinder the
model’s ability to learn effective spatio-temporal dependen-
cies when incomplete neighboring connections are present in
the given spatial graph structure. Therefore, to improve the
generalization ability and adaptability, as well as effectively
handle multiple time series data, we propose a novel
spatio-temporal sequence prediction model LoadSeer.
Tensor time series are advanced, where Transformer is
employed to deal with the multiple time series. LoadSeer
segments and vectorizes the tensor time series data, using the
vectorized sequences as inputs to Transformer. Additionally,
it integrates graph convolutional neural networks to extract
spatial geographic distribution features. Subsequently, further
extracts and combines multiple temporal and spatial evolu-
tion features through a fully connected layer, culminating in
predictions at the output layer. To evaluate the performance
of our proposed method, we compare it with several
well-known spatio-tempora prediction algorithms. Results
demonstrate a significant enhancement in prediction accuracy
using LoadSeer compared to the benchmark algorithms.
To further validate its practicality in real-world scenarios,
we apply LoadSeer to load forecasting in a certain area during
the Asian Games. The experimental results not only reflect
the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm but also verify the
impact of crowd flow on load.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
• We have discovered and verified for the first time
the impact of population mobility on load forecasting
through experiments. Besides, we establish a multi-
dimension spatio-temporal squence data, including
weather, human traffic, history load, and geographical
location information.
• Compared with existing spatio-temporal prediction
methods that can only manage one-dimensional time
sequence and one-dimensional space sequence, we put
forward tensor-based time series, introducing multiple
time series data into spatio-temporal prediction.
• We not only consider geographical location information
in spatio-temporal load forecasting, but also differentiate
land use attributes for the first time, and a distance
adjacency matrix is defined to represent the structure.
We propose LoadSeer, a spatio-temporal sequence
prediction model, to comprehensively consider m

sections.title: RELATED WORK
sections.text:
A. SPATIO-TEMPORAL SQUENCE
Existing methods for modeling spatio-temporal dependencies
can be categorized into three types: spatio-temporal statistics,
artificial intelligence (AI), and physical models. Spatio-
temporal statistics rely on established statistical theories,
such as probability theory, including geographical weighted
regression (GWR) [11], spatio-temporal autoregressive inte-
grated moving average (ST-ARIMA) [12], spatio-temporal
kriging (ST-kriging) [13], and Bayesian maximum entropy
(BME) [14]. Emerging AI methods, such as machine learning
and deep learning, approach spatio-temporal dependencies
from a data-driven perspective [15]. These AI models
have outperformed traditional statistical models in areas
like weather forecasting, traffic prediction, video prediction,
and energy estimation [16], [17], [18], [19], [20]. Physical
models, grounded in physical mechanisms, offer plausible
explanations for forecasted results, but their accuracy can
not match that of statistical and AI models [16], [21],
[22], [23], [24]. Combining AI and physical models can
leverage their respective strengths, enhancing simulation and
forecasting accuracy [25], [26].
B. POWER LOAD FORECASTING
Power load forecasting is crucial for the intelligent man-
agement of power grids. It plays a significant role in
formulating power dispatch plans and enhancing the security
and stability of the grid [27], [28]. In recent years, deep
learning models and hybrid approaches have been extensively
applied in short-term load forecasting due to their ability to
extract abstract features from vast datasets. Notable models
such as one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNN) [29], Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) [30], and Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks [31] have demon-
strated substantial success in this domain. Additionally, the
Temporal Convolution Network (TCN), which leverages
multi-layer causal extended convolution and residual struc-
tures to capture dependencies across different time steps [32],
has shown superior performance compared to LSTM and
GRU [33]. To address the limitations of a single algorithm,
combined models have emerged [34]. For example, a model
integrating GRU with a dual attention mechanism enhances
long-term prediction stability by accurately selecting key
information through the attention block [35]. The CNN-
BiLSTM-Attention model, combining CNN, bidirectional
LSTM (BiLSTM), and an attention mechanism, leverages
data with similar characteristics for training, thus learning
the periodicity and temporal dependencies of the load,
which reduces prediction errors [36]. Another study utilizes
XGBoost and TCN to capture trend characteristics and
nonlinear fluctuations in load series, improving forecasting
performance [37]. Furthermore, the TCN-GRU, designed for
load feature extraction and prediction, has demonstrated the
highest prediction accuracy compared to GRU, LSTM, and
TCN models [38].
Based on the above works, this paper considers the impact
of different factors (population movements, weather, and
historical load) on power load forecasting, and proposes
a novel tensor graph convolutional network for multi-
dimension spatio-temporal squence, LoadSeer. Combining
the structure of time series and spatial geographical locations,
we analyze the load of different land use properties in the
surrounding area.

sections.title: MODEL DESIGN
sections.text:
The overall framework of LoadSeer is illustrated in Figure 1.
LoadSeer comprises three main components: the input
layer, the spatio-temporal processing layer, and the out-
put layer. The input layer receives tensor time series
data X (such as weather, foot traffic, load, etc.) along
with the distance adjacency matrix A, representing the
geographical relationships (such as proximity to commercial
areas, residential zones, hotels, etc.). In the spatio-temporal
processing layer, leveraging the excellent performance of
Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), we extract spatial
features of regions through graph convolutional operations.
Subsequently, the spatial features are concatenated with
multi-dimension temporal data, then are both fed into a T-
Transformer, which captures the spatio-temporal features.
The results are transmitted to the fully connected layer,
where the spatio-temporal features are fitted into a probability
matrix.
A. THE INPUT LA YER
Tensor time series is proposed to capture coordinated changes
among multiple time series, which is highly valuable for
time series prediction and analyzing various variables’
correlations.
Tensor time series is an n+1 mode tensor, denoted as
χ ∈ RI1I2···InT . At time t along the temporal dimension,
the sliced tensor χt ∈ RI1I2···In is an nth-order tensor
containing I1I2 · · ·In data points in the time series. Predicting
the tensor time series χt involves using historical sliced data
χ1, χ2, · · ·, χt to forecast future data at time χT +β :

2) CONCATENATION
The spatial features from the distance adjacency matrix A of
the graph model defined above, maintain spatial relationships
among different regions, including relative positions and con-
nectivity among regions such as commercial areas, residential
areas, and hotel areas. Simultaneously, the time series data
passes through sequence padding, normalization, and feature
extraction to ensure data consistency and comparability. Then
the temporal features are aligned with the spatial features for
subsequent concatenation operations.
3) T-TRANSFORMER
Traditional Transformer typically accepts vectors as input.
However, when dealing with multi-dimensional tensor time
series data, the tensor time series need to be sliced and vec-
torized. The encoded vector sequence is then fed into Trans-
former. This operation transforms the multi-dimensional
features of the tensor time series into multiple vector
sequences for Transformer, thereby combining the vectoriza-
tion of tensor structures with Transformer within a unified
framework. We name it T-Transformer, multi-dimensional
analysis, and prediction problems.
Inspired by Kiers’ Nth-order tensor matrixization method
proposed in 2000 [39], we slice the tensor by the tensor
module k-slicing the tensor is sliced using the tensor mode
k-slicing. That is, the tensor is sliced along the time
dimension to obtain tensor slices for each time point. The
vectorization of the tensor involves column vectorization
and row vectorization. Column vectorization rearranges an
Nth-order tensor χ ∈ RI1I2···In into a column vector of
size (I1I2 · · ·In) 1, commonly denoted as X (I1×I2×···×In)×1 =
vec(χ). Similarly, row vectorization rearranges the tensor into
a row vector.
In the T-Transformer, an embedding operation is per-
formed on the vectorized tensor time series, transforming
it into high-dimensional embedding vectors. However, these
embedding vectors do not inherently contain position
information about the elements in the sequence. Position
encoding can preserve the position relationships of the
sequence elements, thereby enhancing the expressiveness and
performance of the model. We can use the most common
approach, sine and cosine functions, to encode the positions.

sections.title: THE OUTPUT LA YER
sections.text:
The output layer is to fit the spatio-temporal features
obtained from the spatio-temporal processing layer into a
probability matrix and outputs the final prediction results.
This probability matrix reflects the probability distribution
of different prediction targets under different spatio-temporal
conditions. The main task of the output layer is to generate
the final prediction results based on this probability matrix.
Figure 2 shows the overall data processing flow.

sections.title: EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
sections.text:
To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, we first
conduct extensive experiments on several commonly used
public datasets and select multiple evaluation metrics to
observe the results. To further verify its applicability for
power load forecasting during specific events, we establish a
comprehensive spatio-temporal dataset that includes histori-
cal load data, crowd flow, weather conditions, geographical
relationships, and land use properties of different regions
within a certain area during the Asian Games. In this section,
we introduce the datasets, baselines, and evaluation metrics.
Next, the experimental results are provided and analyzed.
A. DATASETS
There are very few public datasets for electricity spatio-
temporal load forecasting, so we choose traffic forecasting
datasets that are similar to load forecasting for the experi-
ments. The PeMSD4, PeMSD7, and PeMSD8 datasets are
commonly used for the evaluation of sequence prediction
methods. These datasets were collected every 30 seconds by
the California Department of Transportation’s Performance
Measurement System (PeMS) [40].
PeMSD4: This dataset is derived from traffic data in the
San Francisco Bay Area, with 307 sensors on 29 roadways.
FIGURE 3. Multi-dimensional Spatio-temporal sequence data.
The dataset covers the period from January to February 2018.
The first 47 days are used for training, while the remaining
days are used for validation and testing.
PeMSD7: This dataset consists of traffic data from
7 districts in California, with 228 sensors. The data covers
weekdays from May to June 2012. The first 34 days serve
as the training set, and the remaining days are allocated for
validation and testing.
PeMSD8: This dataset includes traffic data from San
Bernardino, collected between July and August 2016. There
are 170 detectors placed on 8 roadways. The first 50 days are
used for training, and the remaining time is used for validation
and testing.
Since these datasets only provide one-dimensional time-
series data, we first examine the effect of the proposed method
on one-dimensional time-series forecasting.
To further evaluate LoadSeer on multi-dimensional spatio-
temporal sequence data, as shown in Figure 3, we establish
a real-world electricity load dataset combined with synchro-
nized weather and crowd movement, as well as geographical
location relationships and land use properties around the
venues during the Asian Games. The land is marked as
residential, commercial, and hotel areas. This dataset has
been cleaned and preprocessed by removing outliers, filling
in missing data, and standardizing the values. We refer to
this dataset as Flowload. In this dataset, the load is the
dependent variable, while all other sequence data are treated
as independent variables.
B. DATA PREPARATION
For the above public datasets, in order to divide the data at
a fine-grained level, we follow the method of LSGCN [41]
LSGCN[15] to preprocess. We set the standard time interval
to 5 minutes, and fill in the missing values using linear
interpolation, and normalize the input data using Z-score.

sections.title: BASELINES
sections.text:
In order to evaluate the performance of our proposed
LoadSeer, we compare it with state-of-the-art spatio-temporal
forecasting models (ARIMA, LSGCN, AGCRN, and
ASTGNN).
VOLUME 12, 2024 190341
J. Zhang et al.: LoadSeer: Exploiting Tensor Graph Convolutional Network
ARIMA [42]: introducing seasonal components, the cycli-
cal and trend changes in traffic flow. The model parameters
are estimated using the maximum likelihood estimation
method and validated with actual traffic flow data.
LSGCN [41]: a novel graph attention network called
‘cosAtt’ integrating the graph convolutional network (GCN),
and forming a powerful spatial gating block. By leveraging
this spatial gating block and Gated Linear Unit convolutions
(GLU), LSGCN efficiently captures complex spatio-temporal
features, resulting in reliable prediction results. This inno-
vative combination has significant potential in the field of
spatio-temporal feature analysis.
AGCRN [43]: focusing on learning specific patterns of
individual nodes in traffic prediction tasks and proposes
two adaptive modules: the node-adaptive parameter learning
module and the data-adaptive graph generation module,
which aim to enhance the capabilities of graph convolu-
tional networks to automatically capture fine-grained spatio-
temporal dependencies in the traffic network.
ASTGNN [44]: a novel self-attention mechanism is
specifically designed for transforming numerical sequence
representations in the temporal dimension. This self-attention
mechanism leverages local context to better capture the
temporal dynamics of traffic data.
D. EVALUATION METRICS
Commonly used metrics, such as Root Mean Square Error
(RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Mean Abso-
lute Percentage Error (MAPE), are used for comparative
experiments. RMSE is a widely used metric to measure the
difference between predicted values and actual observations.
It is calculated as the mean of the squared differences between
the predicted and actual values and then taking the square
root of the result. A lower RMSE indicates better prediction
accuracy for the model. MAE is another frequently used
evaluation metric that calculates the mean of the absolute
differences between predicted and actual values. Unlike
RMSE, MAE does not consider the squared errors, thus
focusing more on the absolute differences between predicted
and actual values. MAPE is an evaluation metric expressed as
a percentage. It calculates the mean of the absolute percentage
errors between predicted and actual values. MAPE provides
insights into the relative error magnitude of a model at
different load levels, which is crucial for comparing the
performance of different models.
Considering these three evaluation metrics, the accuracy
and reliability of the models in spatio-temporal forecasting
can be comprehensively assessed. Lower RMSE and MAE
values, as well as lower MAPE values, indicate better model
performance.
E. EXPERIMENTAL RESUL TS
LoadSeer is first compared with four benchmark methods
(ARIMA, LSGCN, AGCRN, and ASTGNN) across three
datasets: PeMSD4, PeMSD7, and PeMSD8. The prediction
horizon is gradually extended, and metrics RMSE, MAE, and
MAPE are collectively used to gauge the predictive accuracy
of the models.
As shown in Table 1, it can be easily observed that
on the three datasets—PeMSD4, PeMSD7, and PeMSD8—
LoadSeer shows competitive performance in MAE, MAPE,
and RMSE metrics. Particularly notable is that in most cases,
LoadSeer achieves SOTA results on all three datasets (except
for MAPE at 15 minutes on the PeMSD4 dataset, MAE
at 15 minutes on the PeMSD8 dataset, and three cases on
PeMSD7), which indicates that our proposed model has a
significant advantage in terms of all the indicators. From the
experiments, our model demonstrates the ability to effectively
control large errors and reduce the negative impact of extreme
values on the overall prediction accuracy, making it perform
exceptionally well in capturing the overall trend and change
pattern of the data, thus improving the stability and reliability
of the prediction results.
It is specifically worth noting that on the PeMSD4 dataset,
LoadSeer reduces the RMSE metric to 2.91 in 60-minute
forecasting, which is 1.92 lower than the previous optimal
value. On the PeMSD7 dataset, LoadSeer reduces the MAPE
to 9.14%. From Table 1, it is evident that LoadSeer achieves
almost optimal results in the MAPE metric on all three
datasets, reflecting its reliability in handling data of different
magnitudes as well as excellent processing logic for both
large and small data values. LSGCN is also competitive
in ultra-short-term prediction due to its LSTM module’s
ability to efficiently capture short-term dependencies and
detail changes through its recursive and gating mechanisms,
while our designed T-Transformer is more inclined to capture
global dependencies, which explains LoadSeer’s excellent
performance in slightly long-term prediction.
To further validate the effectiveness of LoadSeer on
spatio-temporal load forecasting, experiments are conducted
on real data during the Asian Games in a certain region.
As shown in Table 2, LoadSeer exhibits a notable advantage
in terms of RMSE, showcasing its superior overall predictive
capability. ASTGNN achieves the best result in MAPE, with
LoadSeer closely following and a difference of only 0.01.
Nonetheless, the prediction performance of LoadSeer
on real dataset Flowload is very close to the true values

F. ABLATION STUDY
To verify the necessity of the various components of
LoadSeer, we launch ablation experiments on each of them.
VOLUME 12, 2024 190343
J. Zhang et al.: LoadSeer: Exploiting Tensor Graph Convolutional Network
1) ABLATION EXPERIMENTS ON SPATIAL DATA
CORRELATION USING GCN
Unlike traditional time-series forecasting models, we incor-
porate spatial relationship information to more accurately
predict load. By converting spatial information represented
by distance into an adjacency matrix, high-dimensional
and complex spatial information can be quantitatively
represented. Then, the complex spatial information is refined
using graph-based structure modeling and by combining the
advantages of GCN in associating large amounts of data.
To verify the superiority of this new structure, we conduct
ablation experiments on GCN. Without GCN, we compress
spatial information into the same dimension as temporal
information for fusion and perform the ablation experiments
on the PeMSD8 dataset. The results are shown in Table 3.
It can be seen that in the absence of GCN, the model
cannot maintain low losses in RMSE, MAE, and MAPE. The
existence of GCN improves the utilization of the spatial data
in the model, thereby significantly improving the accuracy of
prediction.
TABLE 3. GCN ablation experimental results.
2) FOR ABLATION EXPERIMENTS WITH THE
T-TRANSFORMER
To verify that our designed T-Transformer has excellent
performance, we conduct ablation experiments on it. For
comparison, we choose a universal Transformer architecture
as a substitute. We conduct experiments on the FlowLoad
dataset, which is characterized by multi-dimensional and long
sequences. The dataset can effectively test the model’s ability
to capture and remember information. As shown in Table 4,
our designed T-Transformer has a significant advantage over
the traditional Transformer on long-sequence data. By slicing
and finely modeling the sequences, we can avoid the problem
of being unable to capture distant sequences.
In order to observe the utility of the two different
Transformers in more detail, we conduct experiments on the
T-Transformer and the traditional Transformer for the first
100 time steps. As shown in Figure 7, with the horizontal axis
representing the time steps and the vertical axis representing
the ratio of predicted values to true values, we conduct
several experiments on the two models separately to avoid
randomness. The randomness is represented by shaded lines
in the figure. We select a representative experiment for
marking.
As shown in the figure, our T-Transformer maintains supe-
rior accuracy within 100 time steps. Its accuracy decreases
slowly, reaching about 65 at 100 time steps. Although
the traditional Transformer has accuracy similar to that of
the T-Transformer at short time steps, it decreases rapidly

sections.title: CONCLUSION
sections.text:
In response to the issue of diverse influencing factors
in spatio-temporal prediction, a multidimensional spatio-
temporal forecasting model, LoadSeer, is proposed by
integrating tensor time series with graph convolutional
neural networks. We synthesize information from multiple
dimensions such as time, space, and environment and for
the first time, we take into account the flow of human
beings as an influencing factor, and prove its effectiveness.
The efficient combination of these dimensions, together with
our proposed LoadSeer to accurately capture the impact
of multi-dimensional information on electricity load at
each time period, is demonstrated in multiple datasets and
real-world scenarios of the Asian Games.

sections.title: FUTURE WORK
sections.text:
Although LoadSeer effectively balances power load forecast-
ing accuracy, there are still areas for future exploration. The
scalability of the model could be improved by considering
distributed or parallel computing techniques, especially when
the number of nodes in the graph increases. Moreover,
addressing the decline in accuracy for long forecasting
horizons with multi-scale temporal models could further
enhance its performance in real-world applications. In the
future, we will focus on the above topics for further study.
